name: World Languages: More Practice, Human Judgment
title: World Languages: More Practice, Human Judgment
answer: This idea is that AI can add world language practice when human practice partners are scarce, while teachers keep judgment over feedback and grades. It matters because speaking practice is limited by class time, and writing and pronunciation feedback can be extended, but the evidence is uneven and some tools may miss errors that young learners need to fix.

crumbs.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages

sections.body: Learning a language requires a great deal of practice, and there are not enough partners to practice with. AI can help fill that gap by offering practice in many languages and by letting school configured voice tools hold simple conversations at a student's level. This gives students more speaking practice than a single class period can provide. The problem it solves is scarcity of practice time and partners, not the need for teacher judgment. The idea is to add practice opportunities while keeping human oversight.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: For younger students, Duolingo offers practice for many languages and includes automatic protections for users under 13. School configured voice tools can hold simple conversations with students at their level, which increases speaking practice beyond the class period. In tenth grade, AI feedback on writing in English as a foreign language can support revision and motivation. At university level, AI writing tools have been reviewed in language classes with mixed results. Pronunciation tools can point out incorrect sounds, and detailed feedback on specific sounds appears to help more than general comments, though speech recognition trained mostly on adult native speakers can struggle with young learners.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels the evidence for conversation partners as still thin, and it describes writing feedback in the target language as having stronger support while pronunciation feedback is useful but limited. A small case study of six adult learners found that a voice assistant understood more than 80 percent of their commands while they practiced Japanese on their own (Dizon et al., 2022). In a randomized trial, tenth graders writing in English as a foreign language revised better and felt more motivated after receiving AI feedback (Meyer et al., 2023). A review of AI writing tools in university language classes found mixed results, often from studies tied to the companies that made the tools and rarely with comparison groups (Alharbi, 2023). Speech tools can point out sounds a student is producing incorrectly, and detailed feedback on specific sounds appears to help more than general comments (Bashori et al., 2024), but speech recognition trained mostly on adult native speakers can struggle with young learners and may smooth over the very errors a student needs to fix (Michot et al., 2024).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear in the text. Conversation practice should be treated as a promising idea to pilot rather than a proven method. Speech recognition may miss or smooth over errors, especially for young learners, so the teacher must still listen and judge. Writing feedback design from Chapter 6 applies, with required revision and the grade kept by the teacher. Decisions about feedback, revision and grades stay with a person, and AI does not replace the teacher's judgment.
